statement:
Let $A,B,C$ be three non-collinear points in the plane. Explain briefly why it is possible to choose an origin equidistant from the three points.

Let $O$ be such an origin, let $G$ be the centroid of the triangle $ABC$, let $Q$ be a point such that $\overrightarrow{GQ}=2\overrightarrow{OG}$, and let $N$ be the midpoint of $OQ$.

(i) Show that $\overrightarrow{AQ}$ is perpendicular to $\overrightarrow{BC}$ and deduce that the three altitudes of $\triangle ABC$ are concurrent.

(ii) Show that the midpoints of $AQ$, $BQ$ and $CQ$, and the midpoints of the sides of $\triangle ABC$, are all equidistant from $N$.

[*The centroid of $\triangle ABC$ is the point $G$ such that $\overrightarrow{OG}=\tfrac13(\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{OC})$. The altitudes of the triangle are the lines through the vertices perpendicular to the opposite sides.*]
solution:
**Existence of the origin.** The perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $BC$ are two non-parallel lines, so they meet at a point $O$ equidistant from $A$, $B$ and $C$ (the circumcentre). Take $O$ as origin and write the position vectors as $\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf c$, so that $|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf b|=|\mathbf c|$.

The centroid is $\mathbf g=\tfrac13(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$. Since $\overrightarrow{GQ}=2\overrightarrow{OG}$, we have $\mathbf q-\mathbf g=2\mathbf g$, so $\mathbf q=3\mathbf g=\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c$.

(i) Compute
$$\overrightarrow{AQ}=\mathbf q-\mathbf a=(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)-\mathbf a=\mathbf b+\mathbf c,$$
and $\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathbf c-\mathbf b$. Their dot product is
$$\overrightarrow{AQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)\cdot(\mathbf c-\mathbf b)=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c-|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2-\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf c|^2-|\mathbf b|^2=0,$$
using $|\mathbf b|=|\mathbf c|$. Hence $AQ$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

By symmetry, $BQ\perp CA$ and $CQ\perp AB$. Therefore the lines $AQ$, $BQ$, $CQ$ are the three altitudes (each passes through a vertex and is perpendicular to the opposite side), and they all pass through the single point $Q$. Hence the altitudes are concurrent at $Q$ (the orthocentre).

(ii) The midpoint of $OQ$ is $\mathbf n=\tfrac12\mathbf q=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$.

First, the midpoint of $AQ$ has position vector $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf q)=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)=\tfrac12(2\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$. Its distance from $N$ is
$$\left|\tfrac12(2\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)-\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)\right|=\left|\tfrac12\mathbf a\right|=\tfrac12|\mathbf a|=\tfrac12 R,$$
where $R=|\mathbf a|$ is the circumradius. Identically for the midpoints of $BQ$ and $CQ$ (each gives $\tfrac12 R$).

The midpoint of side $BC$ has position vector $\tfrac12(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$, and its distance from $N$ is
$$\left|\tfrac12(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)-\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)\right|=\left|-\tfrac12\mathbf a\right|=\tfrac12 R,$$
and similarly for the midpoints of $CA$ and $AB$.

Thus all six midpoints (the three midpoints of $AQ$, $BQ$, $CQ$ and the three side-midpoints) are at distance $\tfrac12 R$ from $N$ — these are six of the nine points of the **nine-point circle**, which is centred at $N$ with radius $\tfrac12 R$.
hints: Take the circumcentre as origin, so |a|=|b|=|c|.
Show q = a+b+c using g=(a+b+c)/3 and GQ=2OG.
Use dot products to prove AQ ⊥ BC, and compute distances from N=Q/2.
